title: Substitution reactions of alkanes
keyIdea: In UV light, an alkane reacts with chlorine or bromine by substitution: a halogen atom replaces a hydrogen atom, and the hydrogen leaves as a hydrogen halide. For methane, CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. UV light is needed to split Cl–Cl into two Cl• radicals; a chain of radical steps then repeats until two radicals meet. Because a radical can take any hydrogen, including those in the products, a mixture of CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄ forms.

kid: Alkanes such as methane are not very reactive. But mix methane with chlorine and shine UV light on it, and they react. A chlorine atom takes the place of one hydrogen atom. That swap is called substitution. The hydrogen leaves with the other chlorine atom as HCl.

Why is light needed? In the dark, every bond holds its pair of electrons. UV light has enough energy to split the Cl–Cl bond. That bond is weaker than C–H. Each chlorine atom keeps one electron. An atom with one unpaired electron is called a radical, written Cl•.

A radical wants a partner for its lone electron. Cl• pulls an H atom off methane to make HCl. That leaves •CH₃, which is also a radical. •CH₃ pulls a Cl atom off Cl₂. That makes CH₃Cl and a new Cl•. So the steps go round and round, like a chain. The chain only stops when two radicals meet and join.

Here is the catch. Cl• does not choose. It can take an H from CH₃Cl as easily as from CH₄. So you get CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and even CCl₄ as well. The result is a mixture. Using lots of extra methane makes CH₃Cl the main product.
adult: This topic, for ages 16 to 18, covers free-radical substitution. An alkane and a halogen in UV light give a haloalkane and a hydrogen halide, for example CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. It is often the first mechanism learners meet. It shows how alkanes, with only strong, non-polar σ bonds, can react at all.

Initiation: UV light splits Cl–Cl (about 242 kJ/mol) evenly, one electron to each atom. This is homolytic fission, and it gives two Cl• radicals. The light does not break C–H (about 413 kJ/mol). Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. The radical comes back each time, so one split can make thousands of molecules. Termination: two radicals join to give Cl₂, CH₃Cl or C₂H₆.

Further substitution happens because Cl• can take a hydrogen from any C–H bond in the flask, including those in chloromethane. So the product is a mixture of CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄, which must be separated by fractional distillation. Excess methane makes CH₃Cl the main product. Excess chlorine pushes the mix towards CCl₄.

Common mistakes: writing H₂ instead of HCl as the second product; saying the light breaks the C–H bond; calling Cl₂ → 2Cl• a propagation step; and missing that ethane from termination is evidence for methyl radicals. Take care with curly arrows too: a radical step moves single electrons, so it uses half-headed arrows.

familyTip: Ask: why does the reaction need light, and what does that light actually break? Then count: if every chlorine swaps for one hydrogen, how many HCl molecules come from making CCl₄?

practice.prompt: Methane reacts with chlorine in UV light. What are the products of the first substitution?
choices: CH₃Cl and HCl
CH₃Cl and H₂
CH₂Cl₂ only
practice.hint: One H leaves the methane. What does it join up with?
practice.explain: A Cl atom replaces one H. The H that leaves joins the other Cl atom from Cl₂, making HCl: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.

practice.prompt: Methane is fully substituted by chlorine to make CCl₄. Starting from {n} mol of CH₄, how many moles of HCl form?
practice.hint: Each of the 4 hydrogen atoms leaves as one HCl.
practice.explain: CH₄ + 4Cl₂ → CCl₄ + 4HCl, so {n} mol of CH₄ gives 4 × {n} = {=4*n} mol of HCl.

practice.prompt: Why is UV light needed for methane to react with chlorine?
choices: It splits Cl–Cl into two Cl• radicals
It splits C–H bonds in methane
It removes oxygen from the flask
practice.hint: Which bond is weaker, Cl–Cl or C–H?
practice.explain: Cl–Cl (about 242 kJ/mol) is much weaker than C–H (about 413). UV light splits it homolytically into two Cl•, which start the chain.

practice.prompt: An alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = {n} has its hydrogen atoms replaced by chlorine one at a time. How many substitution steps can happen in total?
practice.hint: Each step replaces one H. Count the hydrogens.
practice.explain: The alkane has 2 × {n} + 2 = {=2*n+2} hydrogen atoms, and each substitution replaces one, so {=2*n+2} steps are possible.

practice.prompt: Which equation is a termination step?
choices: •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl
Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃
Cl₂ → 2Cl•
practice.hint: In termination, radicals go in and none come out.
practice.explain: Two radicals join and no radical is left: termination. Cl• + CH₄ is propagation and Cl₂ → 2Cl• is initiation.

pool.prompt: Which equation is a propagation step?
choices: •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
2Cl• → Cl₂
Cl₂ → 2Cl•
pool.hint: Propagation uses up one radical and makes another.
pool.explain: •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• has one radical in and one out, so the chain carries on: propagation.

pool.prompt: Why does chlorinating methane give a mixture of products?
choices: Cl• can take H atoms from chloromethanes as well as from methane
UV light breaks the carbon atom apart
Chlorine reacts with HCl
pool.hint: Which molecules in the flask still have C–H bonds?
pool.explain: CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃ still have C–H bonds, so Cl• can substitute them again, giving a mixture up to CCl₄.

pool.prompt: How can a chemist make chloromethane, CH₃Cl, the main product?
choices: Use a large excess of methane
Use a large excess of chlorine
Do the reaction in the dark
pool.hint: Make it likely that each Cl• meets CH₄ rather than CH₃Cl.
pool.explain: With far more CH₄ than CH₃Cl in the flask, Cl• almost always hits methane, so further substitution is rare.

pool.prompt: How many moles of Cl₂ are needed to turn {n} mol of CH₄ completely into CHCl₃?
pool.hint: CHCl₃ has 3 Cl atoms in place of 3 H atoms. Each Cl₂ replaces one H.
pool.explain: CH₄ + 3Cl₂ → CHCl₃ + 3HCl, so {n} mol of CH₄ needs 3 × {n} = {=3*n} mol of Cl₂.

pool.prompt: Ethane, C₂H₆, is found in small amounts after methane reacts with chlorine. What does this show?
choices: Methyl radicals, •CH₃, formed and two of them joined
Chlorine contains carbon
The UV light made new carbon atoms
pool.hint: Which termination step gives a two-carbon product?
pool.explain: •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆. Finding ethane is evidence that methyl radicals form during the reaction.

pool.prompt: What kind of bond breaking happens when UV light hits Cl₂?
choices: Homolytic: each Cl atom keeps one electron
Heterolytic: one Cl takes both electrons
No bond breaks
pool.hint: The products are two identical radicals.
pool.explain: The bond splits evenly, one electron to each atom, giving two Cl• radicals. That is homolytic fission.

pool.prompt: Ethane, C₂H₆, reacts with chlorine in UV light until {k} hydrogen atoms have been replaced. How many hydrogen atoms are left on the product?
pool.hint: Ethane starts with 6 hydrogen atoms. Each substitution removes one.
pool.explain: 6 − {k} = {=6-k} hydrogen atoms are left, and {k} chlorine atoms have taken their places.

pool.prompt: A student writes CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + H₂. What is wrong?
choices: The H atom leaves with the other Cl atom as HCl
Nothing is wrong
Methane cannot react with chlorine at all
pool.hint: Count the atoms on each side.
pool.explain: The left side has 4 H and 2 Cl. CH₃Cl + HCl also has 4 H and 2 Cl. CH₃Cl + H₂ has 5 H and 1 Cl, so it does not balance.

visual.caption: Sort each step of the chlorination of methane by its stage.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: switch on UV to split Cl₂, run the radical chain, end it three ways, then steer the product mixture with the Cl₂ : CH₄ ratio.
